strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and comparatively underexplored computer-vision problem: generating automotive radar point clouds from multi-view cameras. The proposed conditional diffusion formulation is a meaningful step beyond deterministic camera-to-radar regression and could help extend visual driving simulators to another sensing modality.

The method is technically coherent. It combines BEV-aligned depth, semantic, and motion priors with joint latent diffusion of density, RCS, and Doppler maps, followed by an explicit sparse deconvolution procedure. The representation is well motivated by the irregular sparsity of processed radar detections.

The experimental evaluation covers several complementary aspects: point geometry, radar attributes, distribution similarity, downstream detection compatibility, scene editing, conditioning ablations, and point-cloud recovery. RadarGen substantially improves over the adapted RGB2Point baseline on most reported metrics, including IoU@1m (0.31 versus 0.23), foreground hit rate (0.66 versus 0.37), and multiple MMD measures.

Evaluating a detector trained only on real radar provides useful evidence that generated samples retain some perception-relevant structure: RadarGen obtains 0.30 NDS, whereas the baseline is effectively unusable. The qualitative scene-editing examples also suggest semantic responsiveness to camera edits and occlusion changes.

The presentation is generally clear, with informative diagrams and visualizations. Training, inference, preprocessing, recovery hyperparameters, and metric definitions are described in useful detail, and the paper explicitly discusses failure modes involving low light, upstream foundation models, and hallucination in unobserved regions.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison is too narrow for the strength of the realism and scalability claims. Evaluation is confined to one train/test split of MAN TruckScenes, one radar configuration, and essentially one adapted baseline. There is no comparison with the closest camera/LiDAR-to-radar approaches discussed in related work, a simple conditional density or occupancy baseline, or other generative point-cloud formulations.

The principal baseline is not fully controlled: RGB2Point receives only time t while RadarGen receives t and t+Δt, is substantially smaller, operates at 224×224 input resolution, emits a fixed 1,024 points, and uses an unnormalized five-channel Chamfer objective because the normalized version reportedly failed to converge. These differences particularly disadvantage its Doppler and density predictions, so the large headline gains do not isolate the contribution of diffusion or the proposed representation.

The central probabilistic-generation claim is insufficiently validated. Quantitative inference uses a fixed seed, while diversity is demonstrated only through a small qualitative figure. The paper does not measure conditional diversity, calibration, coverage, mode collapse, or whether multiple generated samples reproduce the variability of real radar for comparable scenes. Point-level MMD against a single observation is not enough to establish a correct scene-conditional stochastic distribution.

The direct multi-view diffusion ablation complicates the claimed advantage of the BEV foundation-model conditioning: it matches or exceeds RadarGen on DA F1 and several RCS/Doppler MMD values, while many condition-removal effects are extremely small relative to the reported standard deviations. No statistical significance analysis or repeated-training variability is provided, yet the text makes strong claims that every condition is meaningfully used.

The downstream evidence remains preliminary. Relative to real radar, detector performance falls from 0.38 to 0.11 mAP and from 0.48 to 0.30 NDS, with especially poor velocity error. More importantly, the paper evaluates a real-trained detector on synthetic data rather than showing that synthetic radar improves detector training, augmentation, robustness, or simulation-to-real transfer. Thus, practical utility for data augmentation is not established.

Scene editing is evaluated only through a few qualitative, potentially cherry-picked examples without edited-scene radar ground truth, systematic semantic-consistency metrics, or failure statistics. Consequently, these examples support feasibility but not the broad controllability claim.

Generalization and robustness are limited: low-light scenes are explicitly filtered, no cross-dataset or cross-sensor evaluation is provided, and the method depends on camera calibration and three upstream models. Its learned output may therefore reproduce dataset- and radar-processing-specific statistics rather than transferable radar physics.

Reproducibility is only partial. Many hyperparameters are provided, but the manuscript does not state that code, trained models, or preprocessing pipelines will be released. Reproduction would otherwise require multiple large foundation models, a modified 592M-parameter SANA implementation, substantial compute, and a custom IRL1/FISTA recovery pipeline. Overall, the work is promising and close to publishable, but stronger controlled baselines and direct evidence for probabilistic realism and downstream value are needed for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored and relevant computer-vision problem: generating automotive radar observations from multi-view camera imagery. Modeling radar probabilistically and including location, RCS, and Doppler is potentially useful for multimodal simulation.

The overall pipeline is coherent: sparse radar is converted into BEV density and attribute maps, scene-aligned depth/semantic/motion priors provide conditioning, and sparse points are recovered through an explicit deconvolution objective.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished. It supplies useful implementation details, metric definitions, reconstruction ablations, qualitative samples, and an honest limitations discussion covering upstream-model failures and hallucinations.

RadarGen improves substantially over the reported baseline on IoU, foreground hit rate, DA-F1, and most MMD measures. A detector trained on real radar also obtains nonzero performance on generated data, suggesting that the output preserves some task-relevant radar structure.
weaknesses: The experimental comparison is inadequate for the paper's central claim. The sole main baseline is an adapted object-centric RGB2Point model rather than a strong radar-synthesis method. It receives only the images at time t, whereas RadarGen receives t and t+Δt and expensive depth, semantic, and optical-flow priors. It also outputs a fixed 1024 points and was trained for only 18 hours versus RadarGen's 65k-step, two-day training. This does not isolate the benefit of probabilistic radar modeling or establish superiority over suitable alternatives, including the closely related camera-to-radar methods discussed in the paper.

The claimed probabilistic contribution is not convincingly evaluated. Nearly all quantitative results use one fixed seed and compare one generated sample with one observed radar realization. There is no conditional-distribution evaluation across repeated samples, diversity-versus-fidelity analysis, calibration test, mode-collapse analysis, or comparison with a deterministic version of the same architecture. Figure 9 provides only qualitative seed variation.

Several claimed ablation conclusions are unsupported by the numbers. Removing individual BEV conditions changes many metrics only negligibly relative to the reported standard deviations, and direct multi-view conditioning is actually better on several attribute metrics and DA scores. Moreover, zeroing conditions only at inference introduces an out-of-distribution input rather than cleanly measuring what each cue contributes.

Evaluation is restricted to one dataset and radar configuration after excluding low-light night scenes, precisely where radar is especially valuable. There is no cross-dataset, cross-sensor, adverse-weather, or meaningful night evaluation, so the claimed compatibility with broad visual datasets and scalable simulation is not demonstrated.

The downstream evidence is weak: the detector's mAP drops from 0.38 on real radar to 0.11 on RadarGen output, with NDS dropping from 0.48 to 0.30. More importantly, the paper never trains a detector using generated data or measures whether synthetic data improves perception. Thus the asserted simulation/data-augmentation utility is supported only by zero-shot detector evaluation and a few qualitative edits.

The scene-editing application is qualitative and very limited. It lacks quantitative tests of insertion/removal consistency, multi-camera consistency, physical plausibility, and repeated-seed robustness. It is therefore insufficient evidence for controllable simulation.

Despite repeatedly calling the output a 3D radar point cloud, the formal output contains only planar coordinates (x,y), RCS, and Doppler; elevation is discarded. This should be described as a BEV or planar radar point set, and the loss of elevation should be evaluated rather than dismissed without evidence.

The velocity construction is technically underspecified. Differencing independently back-projected points across frames requires careful registration into a common coordinate frame and handling of ego translation/rotation to correspond to radar-relative Doppler. The paper does not clearly state this transformation, leaving uncertainty about physical correctness.

The proposed MMD protocol is unconventional and potentially hard to interpret: bandwidth is adapted from each compared joint point set, entire-area MMD is computed within individual scene pairs, and foreground points are aggregated by class. No sensitivity analysis, confidence testing, or comparison to established generative point-cloud metrics is supplied. Large reported variances further weaken several conclusions.

Reproducibility is only partial. Training hyperparameters are provided, but exact clip splits, preprocessing thresholds for edge removal, semantic color mapping effects, evaluation implementation, and code/model release plans are absent. The pipeline also depends on several large pretrained models and roughly 10.5 seconds per frame on an L40 GPU, tempering the claim of efficient large-scale deployment.

strengths: The paper presents a novel and practically relevant Algorithms/General contribution: probabilistic, scene-level automotive radar point-cloud generation from multi-view cameras, including location, RCS, and Doppler. This is a comparatively underexplored problem with clear value for multimodal driving simulation.

The representation is thoughtful: Gaussian-smoothed density maps, Voronoi attribute maps, latent diffusion, and sparse deconvolution form a coherent solution to the mismatch between sparse radar returns and image-pretrained diffusion models.

BEV-aligned depth, semantic, appearance, and motion cues provide an efficient and interpretable conditioning mechanism. The comparison with direct multi-view conditioning usefully demonstrates a substantial training-time advantage.

Experiments cover geometric, attribute, and distributional fidelity, foreground behavior, reconstruction choices, qualitative examples, stochastic samples, and downstream detection. RadarGen clearly surpasses the adapted RGB2Point baseline on most reported measures, including IoU (0.31 versus 0.23), foreground hit rate (0.66 versus 0.37), and scene-level location MMD (0.056 versus 0.368).

Generated data retain meaningful compatibility with a detector trained on real radar: NDS reaches 0.30, whereas the baseline is effectively unusable. The editing demonstrations also provide compelling evidence of semantic controllability, including changed occlusion patterns.

The manuscript is clear and visually polished, provides detailed metric definitions and implementation hyperparameters, and candidly discusses dependence on upstream foundation models, night-scene failure, hallucination in unseen regions, and the remaining real-to-generated gap.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to one dataset and radar configuration, with low-light night scenes removed. This substantially limits evidence for the claimed broad compatibility with visual datasets and simulators, especially because radar statistics are sensor- and processing-pipeline-specific.

The main comparison is only an adapted, deterministic RGB2Point model originally intended for a different setting. Its fixed 1,024-point output and reported difficulty optimizing the normalized objective may disadvantage it. Comparisons with stronger conditional point-cloud generators, radar density-estimation methods, or simpler probabilistic/count-aware baselines would make the empirical case more convincing.

Despite probabilistic generation being a central motivation, almost all quantitative results appear to use one fixed seed. The paper shows qualitative seed variation but does not measure diversity, coverage, calibration, or best/average performance over multiple samples, so it remains unclear whether the learned conditional distribution is meaningfully superior to a strong deterministic predictor.

The detector result remains well below real radar: mAP is 0.11 versus 0.38 and NDS is 0.30 versus 0.48. Moreover, the study tests a real-trained detector on synthetic data rather than the more simulation-relevant question of whether synthetic data improves training, augmentation, or transfer to real data.

Several proposed metrics and thresholds are newly introduced or selected without sensitivity analysis. In particular, per-example MMD with bandwidth estimated from each compared pair and foreground aggregation can be difficult to interpret, while statistical significance across clips or training runs is not reported.

Condition ablations are performed by zeroing inputs at inference rather than retraining variants, creating a conditioning-distribution shift. Their effects are also small or inconsistent: direct multi-view conditioning performs better on several attribute metrics, and removing individual maps sometimes improves reported MMD values. Thus, the claim that every cue is clearly beneficial is stronger than the evidence supports.

Reproducibility would benefit from an explicit code/model-release statement, exact train/test split identifiers, preprocessing details sufficient to reproduce filtering and projection, and evaluation over multiple training seeds. There is also a likely notation error in the supplementary normalization ranges, where Mp is listed for spatial and Doppler ranges rather than distinguishing the density and Doppler maps.
